summary: Specifies an information model for the Routing Information Base (RIB), the table where routing protocols and configuration place routes before they are installed for forwarding. It supports defining a standard programmatic interface for reading and writing the RIB, as part of the I2RS work.

plainLanguage.summary: A router keeps a big map of which road to take to each place. This describes what that map looks like so programs can read and change it in a standard way.

questions: what is a routing information base
subtitle: Standard data structure for the routing lookup table routers use to forward packets

tldr.problem: Routers need a standardized way to organize and access the Routing Information Base (RIB), which holds routes for packet forwarding. Without a common information model, each router vendor uses their own incompatible format.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines what a RIB should contain: routing instances, routes with match conditions and actions, nexthops with various types (simple, load-balanced, protected, replicated), and the operations (read, write, notifications) that should be supported.
tldr.outcome: A common RIB information model enables standardized programmatic interfaces for centralized control of routing, as used by the I2RS (Interface to the Routing System) working group, allowing controllers to program multiple vendor routers in a consistent way.

today: RFC 8430 is an Informational RFC that provides the information model foundation. The I2RS working group has published RFC 8431, which is the YANG data model for RIB based on this information model, enabling practical programmatic control of routing.

sections.title: Introduction and Use Cases
sections.content:
Routers traditionally manage routes using protocols like OSPF or BGP, which populate the Routing Information Base (RIB). The RIB manager then installs the best routes into the forwarding hardware. However, network operators increasingly need to programmatically control routing based on information beyond routing protocols, such as load on storage or external network data.

The problem is that each router vendor implements the RIB differently, making it impossible to write vendor-independent applications. Reading the RIB requires unreliable methods like per-protocol SNMP MIBs or screen scraping, and writing routes requires vendor-specific configuration. This document specifies a standard information model so a data model can be built to provide a uniform programmatic interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Different routers understand their routing table in different ways, which makes it hard to tell them all what to do. This explains what the routing table should look like so everyone can speak the same language.

sections.title: RIB Structure
sections.content:
The information model describes a hierarchy: a network device contains routing instances, each of which contains RIBs (one per address family like IPv4 or MPLS) and interfaces. A routing instance is a logical slice of the router, useful for modeling VPNs and virtual routing. Within a RIB, each route consists of a match condition (IPv4 destination, IPv6 prefix, MPLS label, MAC address, or incoming interface) and one or more nexthops that specify the action.

Routes have mandatory attributes including route preference (administrative distance), which allows comparing routes from different sources. When an operator programs a static route with lower preference than a protocol route, the static route wins if both lead to the same destination. Routes may also carry vendor-specific attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: A router has multiple routing domains, each with its own routing table. Each table entry says which packets match (where they're going) and what to do with them (where to send them next).

sections.title: Nexthop Types and Complexity
sections.content:
A nexthop can be simple (a physical interface, an IP address, a logical tunnel) or derived for advanced forwarding. A base nexthop can be: an egress interface, an IP address (resolved by the RIB manager), a tunnel encapsulation, or a special nexthop like DISCARD or RECEIVE (for the router itself).

Derived nexthops compose multiple simple nexthops for features like load-balancing (weighted lists), protection (primary and backup with preference), replication (multicast to multiple destinations), and chaining (multiple operations like MPLS pop followed by send to interface). Nexthop indirection allows identifying nexthops by ID, so routes pointing to a BGP peer automatically follow the path if it changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet can go out a single port, or be split across multiple ports for load sharing, or protected with backups that take over when the main path fails, or sent to many places at once.

sections.title: RIB Operations: Read, Write, and Resolution
sections.content:
The RIB manager must support reading entries for RIBs created by a client, and writing (adding, modifying, deleting) entries as well. Clients should write dependencies first (like a nexthop) before routes that use them. The RIB manager must report, for each write, whether the route was installed in the FIB, whether it is active (fully resolved), and the reason if installation failed.

Nexthops can be resolved or unresolved. A resolved nexthop has enough information to forward (e.g., an interface or an IP address on a directly connected neighbor). An unresolved nexthop requires the RIB manager to determine the final path (e.g., reaching an IP address via IGP). Only routes with at least one resolved nexthop are eligible for FIB installation. The RIB manager sends notifications when an unresolved nexthop gets resolved.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell the router where to send packets and ask what routes it knows about. The router tells you whether each path actually works, and sends alerts when something changes.

sections.title: Scaling and Capability Negotiation
sections.content:
The RIB information model must scale to large networks. Bulking (grouping multiple objects in a single message) is MUST for reads and writes, and the RIB manager must handle bulk responses with return codes for each operation. Multiple RIB events can occur simultaneously, and these must be sent in bulk.

Not every network device supports all nexthop types or unlimited recursion levels. The RIB data model MUST provide a way for a RIB client to learn the device's capabilities, such as the maximum number of headers in a chain or whether weighted load-balancing is supported. This capability negotiation is essential so clients can adapt their operations accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: When programs change many routes at once, the router handles them together. Different routers support different features, so programs need to know what each router can do before sending complex instructions.
